claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 exists in a hierarchical-heterostructured state with multilevel chemical fluctuations.
The stated HfNbTiVAl10 state is produced by high-purity arc melting, homogenization, and thermomechanical processing.
The stated processing route ensures multilevel chemical fluctuations in HfNbTiVAl10.
Variance-based atomic descriptors quantify element-specific heterogeneity within an alloy.
Variances in atomic planar density and ionization energy reflect variability in atomic packing and bond strength.
Coarse-grained phase-field simulations can represent microstructural deformation and fracture evolution.
Phase distributions and multilevel chemical fluctuations in the HfNbTiVAl10 heterostructure govern local stiffness and damage evolution.
Combining atomic-feature variance with phase-field outputs supplies complementary atomic- and microstructure-scale information.
The integrated information will allow a surrogate model to capture both elastic behavior and fracture mechanics.
The surrogate will reduce reliance on computationally expensive first-principles and CALPHAD methods.
The integrated model will improve prediction accuracy and computational efficiency for Young's modulus, yield strength, and toughness in hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10.
Conventional approaches have prediction errors of approximately 11–20% for the target properties.
The integrated model will reduce prediction error by approximately 50%, reaching about 5–10% error.
The integrated model will reduce CPU time by roughly one order of magnitude relative to conventional approaches.
Prediction accuracy will deteriorate when processing defects, secondary phases, or other heterostructural states lie outside the training distribution.
The model will lose reliability if the coarse-grained simulation omits fracture mechanisms important to the tested material.
The proposed validation measures Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness experimentally and compares them with model predictions.
The hypothesis is declared falsified if prediction deviation exceeds 20% or computational speedup is less than five-fold.

contradictions.description: The expected accuracy is 5–10% error and the claimed gain is approximately 50%, but the experiment only falsifies errors above 20%. Thus, performance no better than the stated 11–20% baseline could fail to falsify the claimed accuracy improvement.

The expected efficiency gain is roughly ten-fold, whereas the falsification threshold only requires a five-fold gain, so the stated benchmark does not decisively test the quantified efficiency prediction.
